Where it began

Mohammad Yousuf was born in Lahore on 27 August 1974. As a boy he played in the street, with a tennis ball wrapped in tape and a plank of wood for a bat. The Golden Gymkhana took notice of him when he was 12, and later he played at Forman Christian College in Lahore.

His break came in the 1990s, when he was working in a tailor's shop and was picked to play in a local match. His strokeplay caught the eye, and he climbed from there. His first Test was in Durban, against South Africa. In the early part of his career he was known as Yousuf Youhana.

The player

He played 90 Tests for Pakistan between 1998 and 2010, scoring 7,530 runs at 52.29 with 24 hundreds and 33 fifties, the highest of them 223 against England at Lahore in December 2005. He led Pakistan in nine Tests, including a trip to Australia in 2004–05 on which he made a hundred on Boxing Day at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Then came 2006. In England that summer he made 202 in the first Test, 192 at Headingley and 128 at The Oval, and finished the year with more Test runs than anyone had made in a calendar year, beating a record Viv Richards had held for thirty years. He also equalled Don Bradman by making hundreds in six Tests in a row, and needed only four matches to Bradman's six to do it.

What made him special

Ease. He had a high, flowing backlift, lovely timing and an unhurried air at the crease, as if the bowler had been given a little less time than he had. In international cricket he made hundreds against every Test nation and in every one of their countries. In the one-day game he was a sharp fielder too, with a knack for running batsmen out.

He was quick between the wickets, though not always as safe as he was quick: he had a habit of being run out himself. And he was never one for clearing the ropes very often; the runs came anyway.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 2007, and the ICC made him its Test Cricketer of the Year at the 2007 awards. Pakistan honoured him with the Pride of Performance and, in 2011, the Sitara-i-Imtiaz. After his playing days he spent several years passing on what he knew at the National Cricket Academy, and in March 2025 he was appointed batting coach of the Pakistan men's team.

And finally

In 2006 he was dismissed three times in the 190s, and he is the first man in Test history to manage that. Most batsmen would settle for one such near miss in a career. He packed three into a single year, which suggests the 190s were simply where he liked to stop and admire the view.
